name: Postplagiarism Framework (Eaton, 2023)
author: Sarah Elaine Eaton
tenets: Human-AI hybrid writing will become the norm
Creativity can be enhanced by AI
AI can help overcome language barriers
Can outsource writing to AI but not responsibility
Historical definitions of plagiarism require rethinking
dinh_nghia: Eaton's Postplagiarism framework proposes that traditional concepts of plagiarism are becoming obsolete in the age of generative AI. The term 'postplagiarism' does not mean the end of ethical standards; rather, it signals a paradigmatic shift in how authorship, originality, and academic integrity must be conceptualized. In a postplagiarism world, Human-AI hybrid writing is expected and normative, but the writer retains full ethical responsibility for the final output regardless of the degree of AI assistance.
phan_loai: Under the postplagiarism framework, violations are reframed around responsibility and attribution rather than mechanical text-matching. Key categories: (1) Responsibility displacement — submitting AI output while disavowing authorship; (2) Attribution failure — not disclosing AI tools used; (3) Competence misrepresentation — claiming skills one does not possess because AI performed the task; (4) Language barrier exploitation — using AI to mask deficits that assessments are intended to measure. Traditional plagiarism (copying human text without attribution) remains a violation but is treated as a subset of a broader responsibility framework.
lich_su_khai_niem: The term 'postplagiarism' was coined and theorized by Eaton in this 2023 article published in the International Journal for Educational Integrity. The concept builds on Eaton's earlier work including 'Plagiarism in Higher Education: Tackling Tough Topics in Academic Integrity' (2021). It directly responds to the disruption caused by ChatGPT's public release in November 2022 and the inadequacy of existing plagiarism frameworks for AI-generated content.
ten_truong_hop: The postplagiarism framework is primarily theoretical but directly informed by institutional responses in 2023. Key contexts: University of Sydney AI integrity policy (2023), Vanderbilt University ChatGPT statement (2023), and the broader wave of university policy revisions following ChatGPT release in late 2022.
dien_bien: Eaton argues that GenAI tools like ChatGPT fundamentally change the authorship landscape: (1) AI can produce human-indistinguishable text, making traditional text-matching plagiarism detection inadequate; (2) AI can assist non-native speakers in producing fluent academic prose, raising questions about what assessments actually measure; (3) Creativity is not diminished but augmented by AI — just as word processors changed writing, AI changes composition. The six tenets provide a new normative foundation that retains ethical accountability while abandoning outdated definitions.
ket_qua_xu_ly: The postplagiarism framework has been widely cited in the academic integrity literature since 2023. It influenced the development of attribution standards in institutional AI policies. Eaton extended this work in the 'Second Handbook of Academic Integrity' (2024, Springer), which includes a chapter on AI and postplagiarism. Multiple universities referenced the framework when revising their honor codes in 2023-2024.
con_so_thong_ke: Published 2023 in IJEI; 6 core tenets; DOI: 10.1007/s40979-023-00144-1; Eaton's broader academic integrity work spans 2+ books (2021, 2024) and numerous journal articles. The article received significant citation attention given the timing (post-ChatGPT) [uncertain: exact citation count].
hai_cho_nguoi_hoc: The postplagiarism framework identifies a core harm: students who outsource cognitive work to AI fail to develop genuine competencies. Tenet 4 ('Can outsource writing to AI but not responsibility') implies that students who do so face a competence gap — they hold credentials without corresponding skills, which will manifest in professional contexts. Tenet 2 addresses AI-enhanced creativity positively, suggesting that AI used as a cognitive scaffold (rather than a replacement) can benefit learners.
hai_cho_nghien_cuu: Postplagiarism raises research integrity concerns around attribution and hallucinated citations. If researchers use AI to draft papers without disclosure (violating Tenet 6 on attribution), the scholarly record becomes opaque. Eaton's framework implies that all AI-assisted academic work requires provenance documentation — the same standards that apply to data and methods must apply to text generation.
hai_cho_xa_hoi: The postplagiarism era risks devaluing academic credentials if degrees are attained through AI-outsourced work without genuine competency development. Eaton argues this requires reimagining assessment — not simply banning AI — to ensure credentials reflect genuine human capability. The language-barrier dimension (Tenet 3) has social equity implications: AI assistance for ESL students raises both fairness and authenticity concerns.
cong_cu_phat_hien: The postplagiarism framework explicitly challenges the premise of AI detection tools. If Human-AI hybrid writing becomes the norm (Tenet 1), then binary detection (AI vs. human) becomes both technically and normatively inadequate. The framework implies that attribution-based approaches — declaration systems, portfolio evidence, process documentation — are more defensible than detection tools.
han_che_cong_cu: Eaton's framework aligns with Liang et al.'s (Stanford, 2023) findings that AI detectors produce high false positive rates for ESL writers (61.3%). Tenet 3 (AI can overcome language barriers) and Tenet 5 (attribution remains important) together suggest that the appropriate response to language-barrier cases is disclosure and attribution policy, not detection and punishment.
watermarking: LLM watermarking (Kirchenbauer/UMD, Aaronson/OpenAI) would be technically consistent with the postplagiarism framework's attribution tenet (Tenet 5) — watermarks enable provenance tracking. However, Eaton's framework is more concerned with ethical responsibility than technical enforcement; watermarking addresses detection but not the deeper issue of responsibility displacement.
thiet_ke_bai_tap: The postplagiarism framework most directly supports process-based and reflective assessment designs: (1) Staged submissions with process documentation; (2) Reflective journals documenting human cognitive contribution; (3) Oral defense of AI-assisted work; (4) Portfolio-based assessment demonstrating skill development over time. These designs shift evaluation from text output to demonstrable competence and reflective engagement — directly responding to Tenet 4 on responsibility.
chinh_sach_truong_hoc: The postplagiarism framework suggests a tiered disclosure policy rather than blanket prohibition. Eaton's approach aligns with Perkins' AIAS framework (Tiers 3-5 allowing AI with disclosure or integration). Stanford's contextual AI use policy, NUS's disclosure framework (2023-2024), and University of Sydney's AI integrity policy all reflect postplagiarism thinking — retaining ethical standards while adapting to AI reality.
van_hoa_to_chuc: Eaton's framework requires a cultural shift: institutions must move from detection-punishment models to responsibility-attribution models. This aligns with McCabe's honor culture research — students who understand the why of integrity (including AI responsibility) are more likely to comply than those who face only enforcement. Postplagiarism requires faculty education as much as student education.
ai_literacy: Tenet 6 (rethinking historical definitions of plagiarism) directly requires AI literacy education. Students and faculty must understand what AI tools do, how to attribute AI contributions, and what 'authorship' means in a hybrid writing environment. This maps to UNESCO 2023 guidance and EU AI Act Article 4 on mandatory AI literacy.
khung_quoc_te: Eaton's postplagiarism framework is a scholarly contribution from within the academic integrity community rather than a policy instrument. It complements: UNESCO 2023 GenAI guidance (supportive regulation rather than prohibition), ICAI 2021 update (applying 6 values to AI contexts), and Perkins' AIAS framework (tiered AI permission levels). The postplagiarism concept provides the normative rationale for why policy frameworks like AIAS are necessary.
phap_luat_viet_nam: Vietnam's Decree 109/2022 Dieu 20 mandates academic integrity codes but defines plagiarism in traditional terms (text copying) with no reference to AI-generated content. The postplagiarism framework is directly applicable to the gap in Vietnamese law: the responsibility principle (Tenet 4) and attribution principle (Tenet 5) could inform updated Decree language. As of 2024-2025, Vietnam's regulatory framework has not incorporated postplagiarism concepts.
chinh_sach_chau_a: CUHK's 2023 expulsions for AI use, NUS's disclosure framework, and NTU's zero-marks policy for hallucinated citations can all be analyzed through Eaton's tenets: CUHK enforced Tenet 4 (responsibility cannot be outsourced); NUS operationalized Tenet 5 (attribution); NTU applied Tenet 6 (rethinking what plagiarism means when AI fabricates references). Asian institutions are moving from prohibition toward responsibility-based frameworks consistent with postplagiarism.
ai_tutor_vs_ai_cheater: Eaton's postplagiarism framework provides a principled resolution to the tutor/cheater debate: AI is neither categorically a tutor nor a cheater — the determining factor is the human's exercise of responsibility. When students engage critically with AI output, document their cognitive contributions, and attribute appropriately, AI functions as a legitimate intellectual tool. When students displace responsibility and misrepresent AI output as their own competence, it is cheating regardless of technical detection.
edtech_company_policies: Khan Academy Khanmigo (Socratic method, refuses essay completion) embodies Tenet 4 — it requires students to retain cognitive responsibility. Coursera's post-submission dialogue approach operationalizes attribution (Tenet 5) by creating a record of human-AI interaction. The postplagiarism framework provides the theoretical basis for designing EdTech tools that support responsible AI use rather than either enabling fraud or prohibiting AI entirely.
de_xuat_nha_nghien_cuu: From an EdTech researcher perspective applying Eaton's postplagiarism framework: (1) Replace plagiarism detection with attribution verification systems; (2) Redesign assessments to demonstrate process, not just output; (3) Develop AI literacy curricula grounded in responsibility and attribution principles; (4) Update institutional policies to shift from 'AI prohibited/permitted' to 'AI disclosed/undisclosed'; (5) Apply postplagiarism tenets to Vietnam's regulatory gap — use Tenets 4-5 to draft AI attribution standards for Decree 109 updates.

nguon_viet_nam: Eaton's postplagiarism framework has not been formally cited in Vietnamese academic integrity policy documents as of 2024 [uncertain]. The framework is directly applicable to Vietnam's regulatory gap under Decree 109/2022 — particularly as Vietnamese universities begin confronting AI-generated student submissions. No Vietnamese academic has published a Vietnamese-language translation or adaptation of the postplagiarism concept as of early 2026 [uncertain].
